title: Differential psychopathology and patterns of cerebral glucose utilisation produced by (S)- and (R)-ketamine in healthy volunteers using positron emission tomography (PET)

claims.statement: In healthy volunteers given ketamine into a vein in a laboratory, with salt water given to the same people on another day as the comparison, perception, thinking and the sense of self change during the session, and the changes pass within minutes to a couple of hours of the end of the infusion. A 2020 meta-analysis of 36 within-person placebo-controlled studies in 725 healthy volunteers, whose confidence the editors rate low, found higher clinician-rated symptom scores under ketamine than under salt water on every pooled measure: total 1.50 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.77; 25 studies), psychosis-like ('positive') 1.55 (1.29 to 1.81; 21 studies) and withdrawn or blunted ('negative') 1.16 (0.96 to 1.35; 22 studies) standard deviations of the within-person difference, the psychosis-like effect being the larger of the two (difference 0.36, 0.12 to 0.61) (Beck et al., 2020). Those pooled figures are peak values, taken at each study's largest amount and at the rating time with the highest score, so they are the largest effects the studies saw; the studies also disagreed widely about size (I2 65% to 76%) and showed small-study asymmetry (Egger z 4.27 to 5.12), with trim-and-fill estimates of 1.37, 1.49 and 1.09. In the single studies read here the picture is the same. In 18 volunteers (study conditions: 0.1 and 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes, test days in randomized order), scores for conceptual disorganization, hallucinatory behaviour, suspiciousness and unusual thought content rose at the larger amount but not at the smaller or after salt water, as did withdrawal and blunting, dissociation (CADSS) and self-rated perceptual change; the authors state scores returned to baseline generally within 15 minutes of the end of the infusion, and describe what was rated as hallucinatory behaviour as distortions of real stimuli rather than hallucinations (Krystal et al., 1994). In 15 volunteers given a 1-hour infusion the 18-item BPRS total rose from 19.3 (SEM 0.4) to 27.5 (1.6) at 55 minutes and was 21.5 (1.4) at 90 minutes, against 19.1, 18.7 and 18.7 after salt water, carried by thought disorder (3.0 to 6.3) and withdrawal-retardation (3.3 to 6.6) on scales whose floor is 3, while the hallucinations item did not differ (1.2, SD 0.5 against 1.0, SD 0.0; p = 0.190) (Malhotra et al., 1996). In 15 men held at measured steady blood levels, psychosis-like scores and a negative-symptom scale rose with the condition (F3,42 = 21.84 and 10.55), the authors called the syndrome mild, and no abnormal symptoms were found at an abbreviated, unblinded check about 48 hours later (Newcomer et al., 1999). In an open study without a dummy condition, symptoms began on average 4.5 minutes after the start of the infusion (Vollenweider et al., 1997b). What these studies cannot settle is how far the state resembles a psychiatric illness: ego-pathology scores were about two thirds of published values for people with first-episode schizophrenia and two of the five dimensions were clearly less affected, with no patients studied in that paper (Vollenweider et al., 1997a), and the authors of the open study limit their model to the start of acute psychotic episodes. Blinding is the weak point of the whole literature: the visible signs (blurred vision in 8 of 18 people at the larger amount in one study, with nystagmus in about half of them and vomiting in 2) make it unlikely that raters or participants stayed unaware of the condition, and no study read reports a blinding check. All of this describes one session with ketamine in the body in screened volunteers, not repeated or non-medical use.
claims.magnitude: Beck et al. claims.statement: In healthy volunteers scanned while ketamine was being infused, brain activity measured as glucose use, blood flow or the fMRI signal goes up rather than down, and most at the front. In 10 volunteers given racemic ketamine, whole-brain glucose metabolism rose 24.5% (SD 14.3) from each person's own drug-free scan and rose in every participant (p<0.01); the rise was largest in the anterior cingulate (34%) and frontal cortex (30 to 34%) and smallest in the occipitomedial cortex (16 to 17%), with no decrease in any region examined, and front-to-back ratios shifted accordingly (Vollenweider et al., 1997b). In a second group of 10 given the (S)-form, regional increases ran from 19.6% in the frontomedial to 27.35% in the parietal cortex, with cortical regions about 2 to 3 times more affected than deeper structures and the whole-brain change (12%) not reaching significance (Vollenweider et al., 1997a). A 2024 meta-analysis that pooled the published peak coordinates of 33 functional-imaging studies in 628 healthy volunteers, and whose confidence the editors rate critically low, found only two clusters that survived correction for multiple testing: more activity at rest in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (658 voxels, 495 after correction) and, during executive-function tasks, in the right Heschl's gyrus (160 voxels, 142 after correction); across all 23 task studies together nothing was significant and no decrease was found in any analysis (Ait Bentaleb et al., 2024). What these scans cannot show is which change produces which experience: both 1997 studies report every symptom-to-brain correlation as a significance level with a direction and print no correlation coefficient anywhere, they made about 150 to 180 comparisons without correcting for their number and call the analysis exploratory, one of them had no dummy condition and in the other every participant recognised the drug. All of this describes a single session with ketamine in the body, not any lasting change.
claims.magnitude: Vollenweider et al. (1997b), racemic, n=10: whole-brain glucose metabolism +24.5% (SD 14.3, Wilcoxon p<0.01, higher in every participant); cingulate anterior +34%, frontal +30 to 34%, insula +19 to 23%, parietal +18 to 25%, somatosensory +19 to 25%, motor +15 to 18%, temporal +16 to 19%, occipitomedial +16 to 17%; no decreases. Frontomedial/temporomedial ratio 1.31→1.44 (left) and 1.41→1.53 (right), frontomedial/occipitomedial 1.04→1.14 and 1.06→1.16 (all p<0.05). Vollenweider et al. (1997a), (S)-ketamine, n=10: frontomedial +19.6%, frontolateral +20.1%, cingulate anterior +23.5%, cingulate posterior +24.0%, parietal +27.35%; thalamus +17% (p<0.07); whole brain +12% (p<0.09, not significant). Ait Bentaleb et al. (2024): resting state, left anterior cingulate/paracingulate BA 24 (MNI 0; 30; 20), Z=4.265, p<0.001, 658 voxels, 495 after correction; uncorrected only, right insula BA 47 (36; 24; −6), Z=3.432, 30 voxels, and right fusiform gyrus BA 30 (22; −34; −16), Z=2.933, 26 voxels. Executive-function tasks (9 studies): right Heschl's gyrus BA 48 (44; −16; 6), Z=3.306, 160 voxels, 142 after correction; uncorrected right rostral anterior cingulate BA 10 (6; 52; 8), Z=2.889, 26 voxels. No effect size or interval is recoverable from a coordinate-based meta-analysis.

claims.statement: In 10 healthy volunteers who received, a month apart and in counterbalanced order, a placebo scan, (S)-ketamine and an equimolar amount of (R)-ketamine, the two mirror-image forms did different things. (S)-ketamine produced a short-lived psychosis-like state: depersonalisation and derealisation, visual disturbances from pseudohallucinations to complex hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy, with heightened feelings or euphoria reported by 30%, indifference by 30% and heightened anxiety by 40%, alongside higher scores for deactivation, introversion, emotional irritability and anxiety on a mood scale. The same people on (R)-ketamine reported no psychotic symptoms but a state of relaxation, with only trend-level changes on the scales. Every one of the 10 scored higher under (S)- than under (R)-ketamine on both global scales (altered-states score 37.0, SD 12.6, against 15.6, SD 8.6; ego-pathology score 24.6, SD 11.8, against 1.3, SD 1.6). The brain scans went in opposite directions: (S)-ketamine raised glucose metabolism across most regions, while (R)-ketamine tended to lower it, significantly in the temporomedial cortex on both sides (−13.4%) and the left insula (−14%). Blood levels were similar in the two conditions (mean 379 ng/mL, SD 71, against 389, SD 74) (Vollenweider et al., 1997a). Three things limit this. The blind did not hold: every participant recognised the (R)-ketamine condition as a drug effect, and all had had an (S)-ketamine session beforehand. The two forms were not compared with the racemic mixture in these same people, and the paper's description of the (S) condition as 60% of the racemic amount used earlier does not match the infusion rates printed in the two papers, so its conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetic part of racemic ketamine goes beyond what was measured here. And a separate three-person study found no significant difference between the forms in how the body handles them, which with three people and no test statistic says very little (Yanagihara et al., 2003). A 2016 review reports, second-hand, that S-ketamine has about four times the affinity of R-ketamine for the NMDA receptor and has been postulated to be about four times as potent as R-ketamine and twice as potent as the racemate, that R-ketamine slows the elimination of S-ketamine (clearance 26.3 mL/kg/min for S-ketamine alone against 18.5 for the S-form inside the racemate in ten healthy men), and that the two forms differ in reported side effects.
claims.magnitude: Vollenweider et al. (1997a), n=10, within-person: altered-states global score 37.0 (SD 12.6) under (S)-ketamine against 15.6 (SD 8.6) under (R)-ketamine; ego-pathology global score 24.6 (SD 11.8) against 1.3 (SD 1.6); higher under (S) in all 10 participants (editors' calculation of the within-person difference: 22.6 points, SD 6.3, and 23.3 points, SD 10.9; exact two-sided sign test p = 0.002). Emotional reactions under (S): euphoria or heightened feelings 30%, indifference 30%, heightened anxiety 40%. (R)-ketamine: no psychotic symptoms; oceanic boundlessness p<0.06, well-being p<0.09, emotional irritation p<0.08. Glucose metabolism under (R): whole brain −9.8% (p<0.07, not significant), temporomedial cortex −13.4% bilaterally and left insula −14% (p<0.05). Blood levels 269 to 523 ng/mL (mean 379, SD 71) under (S) and 280 to 508 (mean 389, SD 74) under (R).
